note: General heuristics for the model method: how to choose the model from clues in the question, how to break a problem down, the traps, and what to do when stuck. Written for a P6 reader.

thinking.title: Four thinking moves that work on every problem
thinking.intro: These are the same four moves a programmer uses. They are not maths tricks; they are ways of handling something too big to hold in your head all at once.

moves.name: Break it up
moves.plain: Cut one big problem into small ones you already know how to do.
moves.inMaths: A 4-mark problem is almost never one step. It is three easy steps wearing a coat. Find the first easy step and do only that.
moves.prompt: What is the smallest thing I could work out right now, even if it is not the answer?

moves.name: Spot what repeats
moves.plain: Look for the same shape of thing happening again.
moves.inMaths: If you have met a problem where a total stayed the same while things moved around, this one may be the same problem with different names and numbers.
moves.prompt: Have I seen this shape before? What was it called?

moves.name: Keep only what matters
moves.plain: Throw away the story. Keep the numbers and the relationships.
moves.inMaths: It does not matter that they are marbles or that his name is Ali. What matters is: two quantities, one is 27 more, the total is 141.
moves.prompt: If I rewrote this in ten words with no names, what would it say?

moves.name: Follow the steps
moves.plain: Once you know the type, there is a fixed order that works every time.
moves.inMaths: Every model type on this site has a set order. Learn the order and you stop having to be clever under pressure.
moves.prompt: What is step one for this type? Do that first, before thinking about the answer.

fifth.name: Check it back
fifth.plain: Put your answer into the story and see if the story still makes sense.
fifth.inMaths: If Ali ends with 84 and Ben with 57, is Ali really 27 more? Does the total really come to 141? Thirty seconds here catches most careless marks.
fifth.prompt: Does my answer make the original sentences true?

deconstruct.title: The six-step routine
deconstruct.intro: Do these in order every time, even when the problem looks easy. The order is what protects you when it is not.

steps.name: Read twice, differently
steps.do: First read for the story: who is involved and what happens. Second read with a pencil: circle every number and underline every relationship word.
steps.why: One read tries to do both jobs and does neither. Most misread problems are misread on the first sentence.

steps.name: List the characters
steps.do: Write the names or quantities down the side of your working. Two names means two bars. Three names means three bars.
steps.why: Deciding how many bars before you draw stops the model from growing extra bars halfway through.

steps.name: Find the time line
steps.do: Ask: is there a before and an after? Look for at first, then, after that, in the end, finally.
steps.why: If there is a before and an after you need two models, one above the other. Trying to fit both into one model is the commonest reason a model goes wrong.

steps.name: Find what does not change
steps.do: Ask the three questions: is the TOTAL the same before and after? is the DIFFERENCE the same? is ONE quantity the same? Write it down.
steps.why: This single answer chooses your model type. It is the most important line you will write, and most students never write it.

steps.name: Draw and label
steps.do: Draw the bars roughly to scale. Put every number you know on the model. Put a question mark on what you want.
steps.why: A model with no numbers on it is a picture, not a tool. Roughly to scale matters: if a bar that should be bigger looks smaller, you will misread your own drawing.

steps.name: Answer the question that was asked
steps.do: Go back to the last sentence of the problem. Underline exactly what it wants. Check your units.
steps.why: Finding the value of one unit is not the answer. It is the step before the answer. Marks are lost here more than anywhere else.

invariant.title: What stays the same tells you which model
invariant.intro: This is the single most useful table on this page. When a problem has a before and an after, something almost always stays the same. Find it and the model chooses itself.

rows.clue: Something moves from one person to another, but nothing enters or leaves the group.
rows.draw: Draw one long bar for the total, twice: once split before, once split after. The whole bar has the same length both times.

rows.stays: The TOTAL stays the same, with some quantities fixed
rows.clue: Part of the group does not take part in the change at all.
rows.draw: Draw the fixed part as a block you never cut, and do the working only on the part that moves.

rows.clue: The same amount is added to both, or taken from both.
rows.draw: Draw the two bars with the gap between their ends marked. That gap is the same length in the before model and the after model.

rows.stays: The DIFFERENCE stays the same, because time passes
rows.clue: Ages. The gap between two people's ages never changes.
rows.draw: Same as Same Difference. The trap is thinking that if one doubles, the other doubles. Only the gap is fixed.

rows.clue: Only one person's amount changes; the other is untouched.
rows.draw: Draw the unchanged bar the same length in both models, and use it as your ruler.

rows.clue: After the change, both have the same amount.
rows.draw: Draw the after model FIRST, as two equal bars. Then work backwards to the before.

rows.clue: Before the change, both had the same amount.
rows.draw: Draw the before model first as two equal bars, then apply each change.

rows.clue: Both change, by different amounts, but a relationship is given at the end.
rows.draw: Use the AFTER relationship to set your units, then work backwards. Units come from the sentence that has as many as in it.

chooser.title: Identifiers: what the words are telling you to draw
chooser.intro: Before deciding anything else, find these words. They are the strongest signal in the question.

groups.when: You are told a total, or asked for a total. Nothing is being compared.
groups.draw: One bar cut into parts. The whole bar is the total.
groups.watch: The rest and the remainder mean what is left AFTER the earlier parts are taken out, not a fraction of the original.

groups.when: Two or more quantities are being set against each other.
groups.draw: Two bars, one above the other, left ends lined up. The extra sticking out is the difference.
groups.watch: Read the direction carefully. A has 27 more than B is not the same as A has 27, B has more.

groups.when: One quantity is a whole number of times another.
groups.draw: Draw the smaller quantity as ONE unit, and the larger as that many equal units.
groups.watch: Twice as many as B means A is 2 units and B is 1 unit, so the total is 3 units, not 2.

groups.when: A fraction is applied to something.
groups.draw: Cut the bar into the number of parts in the denominator. If a second fraction is of the remainder, cut only the leftover piece.
groups.watch: Of the remainder is the biggest trap in P6. The second fraction is a fraction of what is LEFT, not of the original total.

groups.when: Items have both a count and a price or value.
groups.draw: Two rows: one for how many, one for how much. Keep them separate or you will multiply the wrong pair.
groups.watch: Never add a number of coins to an amount of money. Count and value are different kinds of thing.

groups.when: The same situation is described twice with different numbers.
groups.draw: Two models, one for each case, stacked. Compare them to find the difference the change made.
groups.watch: The useful step is the DIFFERENCE between the two cases, not either case on its own.

groups.when: Several equal groups make a total.
groups.watch: Check whether the total given includes the group you are asked about, or excludes it.

traps.name: Answering the step, not the question
traps.looks: You find the value of 1 unit and stop, or you find the before amount when the question asked for the after.
traps.avoid: Before writing the final line, reread only the last sentence of the problem and underline the noun it asks for.
traps.cost: This costs more marks than any actual maths error.

traps.name: Of the remainder
traps.looks: Treating one third of the remainder as one third of the original.
traps.avoid: Draw the first cut. Shade what is used. Then cut ONLY the unshaded piece for the second fraction.
traps.cost: The whole answer is wrong, not just the last step.

traps.name: Units that are not the same size
traps.looks: One bar uses units of 5 and the other uses units of 3, but you count them as the same.
traps.avoid: When two different unit sizes appear, make them the same size first by finding a common multiple, then redraw.
traps.cost: The model looks right and the answer is wrong, which is the hardest kind of mistake to spot.

traps.name: Assuming equal when it is not stated
traps.looks: Splitting a bar into equal parts because it is tidy, when the problem never said the parts were equal.
traps.avoid: Only draw equal parts if the problem uses each, every, equally, or a multiple.
traps.cost: You solve a different, easier problem than the one on the paper.

traps.name: Both quantities change but you keep the difference
traps.looks: Using Same Difference when one person gained 5 and the other gained 8.
traps.avoid: Same Difference only holds when the SAME amount is added to both or taken from both. Check the two numbers are identical.
traps.cost: Wrong model type from step four onwards.

traps.name: Losing the units of measure
traps.looks: Mixing centimetres and metres, or minutes and hours, inside one model.
traps.avoid: Convert everything to the smaller unit before drawing anything.
traps.cost: Arithmetic is right, answer is out by a factor of ten or sixty.

traps.name: Reading the comparison backwards
traps.looks: A has 12 fewer than B, drawn as A being longer.
traps.avoid: Say the sentence aloud with the bigger one first: B is bigger, so B's bar is longer.
traps.cost: Every step after the drawing is wrong.

traps.name: Drawing before reading to the end
traps.looks: Starting the model after the second sentence, then having to erase.
traps.avoid: Read all the way to the question mark before the pencil touches the paper.
traps.cost: Time, and a messy model you then misread.

assumptions.title: Things you are allowed to assume, and things you are not
allowed: That quantities cannot be negative. Nobody has minus three marbles.
That counts of objects are whole numbers unless the problem is about measurement.
That when a problem says shared equally, the parts really are identical.
That the diagram is not to scale unless it says so, so never measure it.
notAllowed: That two people started with the same amount, unless it says so.
That a fraction refers to the original total, when the sentence says remainder.
That a change applies to everyone, when only one person is named.
That the answer must be a tidy number. Some are not, and doubting a correct untidy answer wastes time.

reframe.title: When you are stuck, change the question
reframe.intro: Being stuck is normal and is not a sign you cannot do it. It usually means you are looking at the problem from the wrong end. These six moves change where you are standing.

moves.name: Work backwards
moves.do: Start from the end state, which is usually the tidiest, and undo each step.
moves.useWhen: The problem ends with something equal, or with a known final amount.

moves.name: Make the units the same
moves.do: If one bar is in thirds and another in quarters, cut both into twelfths.
moves.useWhen: Two different fractions or ratios appear and you cannot compare them.

moves.name: Add something imaginary
moves.do: Pretend to give the smaller person enough to make them equal, then take it back at the end.
moves.useWhen: Two quantities are nearly equal and the gap is known.

moves.name: Try a small number
moves.do: Guess a simple value for one unit, run the story, and see how far off you land.
moves.useWhen: You understand the story but cannot see the first step. This often reveals the relationship.

moves.name: Swap what you call one unit
moves.do: You chose the wrong bar as one unit. Choose the other one and redraw.
moves.useWhen: Your units come out as fractions instead of whole numbers.

moves.name: Rewrite it in ten words
moves.do: Strip the names and the story until only the maths is left.
moves.useWhen: The problem is long and you have lost track of what it is actually asking.
